title: She's Taking Down Her Own Father's Empire. Telugu's Darkest New Crime Saga Just Landed on Prime Video.
excerpt: Isakapatnam drops Aishwarya Rajesh into a 1990s port town ruled by blood and politics — streaming now in Telugu, Hindi, and Tamil with English subtitles worldwide.
body:
There's a particular kind of crime drama that South Indian cinema does better than anyone. Not the slick, English-subtitled prestige thriller — the raw, blood-on-the-docks kind, where every frame smells like diesel and betrayal. Isakapatnam, which dropped on Amazon Prime Video today, is reaching for exactly that register.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=5ZwG-8JBlos

Set in a fictional 1990s port town inspired by Visakhapatnam, the seven-episode series follows the rise and reckoning of Naidu — played by the formidable Samuthirakani — a man who arrived as a nobody and clawed his way to the throne by killing the town's reigning crime lord. He controls the shipping lanes, the politicians, and the police. He controls everything, in fact, except his own daughter.

That daughter is Bharati, played by Aishwarya Rajesh, and she is the heartbeat of this show. Bharati doesn't approve of her father's empire. She doesn't want to reform it. She wants to dismantle it from within — a premise that borrows from the DNA of Vada Chennai and KGF but stakes its emotional claim on something rarer in the genre: a woman who isn't the collateral damage. She's the detonator.

"Portraying Bharati was both challenging and deeply rewarding. She is a woman with immense agency and conviction, refusing to be defined by her circumstances while embracing both vulnerability and courage." — Aishwarya Rajesh

Aishwarya Rajesh has earned the right to carry a show like this. From Kanaa to Vada Chennai to World Famous Lover, she's built a career defined by a refusal to coast on the expected — and in Isakapatnam, she brings that same coiled intensity. Opposite her, Samuthirakani plays Naidu with the quiet menace of a man who's spent decades winning and can't recognise when the ground is shifting beneath him. Their dynamic — father-daughter, predator-protector, king-and-insurgent — is the engine that drives every episode.

The supporting cast is stacked. Sunil — in a dramatic turn that's worlds away from his comedy roles — plays a character whose loyalties are pulled in competing directions. Naresh Agastya delivers a promising performance as a young man striving to rise above his circumstances. Jwala Koti, Banerjee, and Sudhakar Komakula round out the ensemble with the kind of lived-in intensity that period crime demands.

Director Garry BH — better known as a respected editor on several Telugu hits — makes his directorial debut here, and it shows in the right ways. Cinematographer Vamsi Patchipulusu gives the port town a humid, sepia-toned atmosphere — all rust, fluorescent light, and monsoon grime — while Pravin Lakkaraju's score leans into the menace without overdoing it. The '90s setting is key: this is pre-liberalisation India, where power was raw, rules were unwritten, and the law bent for anyone who could afford it.

Is it perfect? Not quite. Early reviews suggest the writing doesn't always match the ambition of its performances. The plot leans on familiar crime-drama beats — rival factions, shifting loyalties, a final reckoning — and some episodes lose momentum in the middle stretch. The pacing occasionally slows when the show could use a knife. But the performances carry you through the weaker stretches, and when Isakapatnam locks into its rhythm — Samuthirakani staring down a rival, Aishwarya making a choice that can't be undone — it hits with genuine force.

Here's the case for diaspora viewers: Isakapatnam is streaming globally on Prime Video with Hindi and Tamil dubs and subtitles in 15 languages, including English. If you've been waiting for the next Telugu crime saga after Pushpa rewired your brain and Vada Chennai ruined every other gangster film for you, this is the closest thing on the streaming calendar right now. Seven episodes. No theatrical window to wait out. It's already on your screen.

The performances alone — especially the Samuthirakani-Aishwarya Rajesh dynamic — justify pressing play. And the central question — what happens when the one person who can destroy an empire is the one who was raised inside it — is the kind of hook that keeps you watching past midnight.

Seven episodes. One port town. One empire worth burning down.
